Story · Lesson 1

The Talk in Cairo

Sara arrives in Cairo to give the most important talk of her life, but her laptop is still on the plane. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of a journalist in the audience.

Join ideas with participle clausesTell a story in a formal styleTalk about turning a problem into a chance

1The story

Having landed in Cairo at two in the afternoon, Sara took a taxi straight to the conference center. Her talk on solar water pumps was at five, and she had spent three weeks preparing it. Everything was on her laptop, forty slides, photos of the village, and a short video of the pump.

Arriving at her hotel, she opened her bag to check her notes. Her laptop wasn't there. Her heart sank. Thinking back, she could see it clearly, in the seat pocket on the plane, exactly where she had left it.

She called the airline. The plane had already left for Dubai. Not knowing what else to do, she called Omar. "Do you have a copy of the slides?" she asked. "No," he said. "But you don't need slides. You need the story. You were there."

Left with only a pen and a notebook, Sara sat in a café near the conference center and wrote five words on a page. Water. Walk. Sun. Flood. People. Encouraged by Omar, she decided to make the most of it.

At five o'clock, she walked onto the stage. The screen behind her was empty. "I was going to show you forty slides," she began, "but my laptop is flying to Dubai without me." The audience laughed, and she relaxed.

Then she told them a story. She told them about the women who used to walk two hours a day for water, and about the morning the pump started. She told them about the night the river rose, when the batteries from the pump lit the school. Speaking without slides, she looked at the audience, not at a screen, and the audience looked back.

When she finished, there was a moment of silence, and then the whole room stood up and clapped. Asked later by a journalist about her missing laptop, Sara smiled. "Every cloud has a silver lining," she said. "With my slides, I would have talked to a screen. Without them, I talked to people."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
When did Sara land in Cairo?At two in the afternoon.
2
What was her talk about?Solar water pumps.
3
How long had she spent preparing it?Three weeks.
4
What did she find when she opened her bag?Her laptop wasn't there.
5
Where had she left the laptop?In the seat pocket on the plane.
6
Where was the plane going?To Dubai.
7
What did Omar say she needed?The story, not slides.
8
What five words did she write?Water, walk, sun, flood, and people.
9
How did she begin her talk?"I was going to show you forty slides, but my laptop is flying to Dubai without me."
10
What did she tell the audience about?The women who walked for water, the morning the pump started, and the night the river rose.
11
What did the audience do when she finished?They stood up and clapped.
12
Why does Sara think losing the laptop was good?Without her slides, she talked to people, not to a screen.

3Point of view Now Rania, a journalist, tells it.

R

I have reported on conferences for ten years, and most talks are the same. Having seen hundreds of slides, I usually sit at the back and check my phone.

That afternoon, a young engineer walked onto the stage with nothing in her hands. Seeing the empty screen, I expected a disaster. Instead, she made us laugh in the first ten seconds.

Listening to her, I forgot to take notes. She talked about real people, and she spoke as if she were telling the story to friends.

Asked by my editor which talk was the best of the conference, I didn't need to think. It was the one with no slides at all.

4What did you learn?

You learned participle clauses.

They make sentences shorter and more formal. The subject of the clause is the same as the subject of the main sentence.

Participle clauseWhat it means
Having landed, she took a taxi.After she had landed, …
Arriving at her hotel, she…When she arrived at her hotel, …
Not knowing what to do, she…Because she didn't know what to do, …
Left with only a pen, she…Because she was left with only a pen, …
Asked about her laptop, she…When she was asked about it, …
-ing: active, at the same timeSpeaking without slides, she looked at the audience.
Having + past participle: beforeHaving seen hundreds of talks, I sat at the back.
Past participle: passiveEncouraged by Omar, she decided to try.
QuestionsWhat do you usually do, having finished a long day?Having finished work, I usually drink tea with my family.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomyour heart sinks

you suddenly feel sad or worried

When I saw the long line at the bank, my heart sank.
phrasemake the most of something

to use a situation as well as you can, even when it is not perfect

It rained all week, but we made the most of it and visited the museums.
proverbEvery cloud has a silver lining.

Something good can come from even a bad situation.

I lost my job, but I found a better one. Every cloud has a silver lining.

6New words

slidespages that are shown on a screen during a talk
stagethe raised place where a speaker stands
audiencethe people who watch or listen to a talk
relaxedbecame calm and less nervous
journalista person who writes news for a newspaper or website
editorthe person who decides what a newspaper prints

Topic · Lesson 2

How to Give a Great Talk

Most people are afraid of speaking in public. A few simple steps can make any talk better.

Talk about public speakingGive advice in a clear orderUse participle clauses in advice

1Read

Many people say that they are more afraid of public speaking than of spiders, snakes, or flying. Their hearts beat fast, their hands shake, and their minds go blank. But giving a good talk is a skill, and like any skill, it can be learned.

Start with your audience. Who are they, and what do they need to know? Having answered that question, choose one main message. A talk with ten messages is remembered for none of them.

Next, build your talk around a story. People forget numbers and lists, but they remember stories, especially true ones about real people. Begin with something that will break the ice, a question, a surprising fact, or a little humor, and then get to the point quickly.

Use slides carefully. A slide should show a picture or a few words, not a page of text. If the audience is reading, they are not listening. And always be ready to speak without them, because technology fails more often than you think.

Finally, practice aloud, not just in your head. Record yourself on your phone and time your talk. Speak more slowly than feels natural, and pause after important points. Look at people, not at the screen or the floor.

Being nervous is normal, even for experienced speakers. The trick is not to stop the fear but to use it. Having prepared well, you will find that a little fear gives you energy instead of taking it away.

2Four steps to a great talk

1Audiencewho are they, and what do they need?
2Messagechoose one main idea
3Storybuild the talk around real people
4Practicealoud, with a timer

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
What are many people more afraid of than spiders?Public speaking.
2
What should you think about first?Your audience.
3
Why should a talk have only one main message?A talk with ten messages is remembered for none of them.
4
Why should you build a talk around a story?People forget numbers and lists, but they remember stories.
5
What should a slide show?A picture or a few words.
6
How should you practice?Aloud, recording yourself and timing the talk.
7
What does a little fear give you?Energy.

4Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiombreak the ice

to say or do something that helps people relax at the start

Our teacher broke the ice on the first day with a funny game.
phraseget to the point

to talk about the most important thing without wasting time

We only have five minutes, so please get to the point.

5New words

blankempty, with no ideas
skillsomething you can do well because you have learned it
humorthe quality of being funny
pausestop for a short time
experiencedhaving done something many times
energythe power and strength to do things

Conversation · Lesson 3

Questions From the Audience

Answering questions clearly and honestly after a talk

Welcome and answer questionsSay that you will check a factClose a question time politely

1Read the conversation

After her talk in Cairo, Sara takes questions from the audience. Dr. Kamal, a professor of engineering, and Rania, a journalist, ask her questions.
DKDR. KAMALThank you for a wonderful talk. How much does one pump cost, and who pays for it?
SSARAThat's a great question. The whole system cost less than a small car. This time, the money came from our university and a local business.
DKDR. KAMALAnd what happens when something breaks? Who repairs it?
SSARAWe trained two young people from the village to look after it. Having learned the basics, they can fix most problems themselves.
RRANIACould this work in other countries, too?
SSARAI believe so, especially where there's a lot of sun and the water isn't too deep. But I'd rather not guess the numbers. Let me get back to you on that after I check.
RRANIAOf course. And what was the hardest part of the project?
SSARAHonestly, it wasn't the engineering. It was listening. We had to understand what the village needed before we built anything.
DKDR. KAMALThat's certainly food for thought for all of us engineers.
SSARAThank you. If there are no more questions, I'll be outside if anyone would like to talk.

2Useful phrases

Welcome a question

That's a great question.

Give a clear answer

The whole system cost less than a small car.

Say that you will check

Let me get back to you on that after I check.

Be careful with facts

I'd rather not guess the numbers.

Answer honestly

Honestly, it wasn't the engineering. It was listening.

Close the questions

If there are no more questions, I'll be outside.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phraseget back to someone

to answer someone later, when you have more information

I don't know the price yet, but I'll get back to you tomorrow.
idiomfood for thought

an idea that makes you think carefully

His talk about saving water gave us all food for thought.

4New words

localfrom the area near you
trainedtaught someone the skills for a job
basicsthe simplest and most important things to know
engineeringthe work of designing and building machines and structures
honestlytelling the truth
certainlywithout any doubt

Story · Lesson 4

The Night the River Rose

A sudden flood cuts off the village where Sara's team built its solar pump. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of an engineer on her team.

Give emphasis with inversionTell a dramatic storyDescribe how people work together in a crisis

1The story

Sara had visited the village near Kassala many times since her team built the solar pump, but she had never seen the sky like this. Never had the old men of the village seen so much rain in one afternoon. By evening, the Gash River, which is dry for most of the year, had become a brown, roaring wall of water.

Not only did the river rise faster than anyone expected, but the road to Kassala was also cut off within an hour. Fifty families lived on the low side of the village, close to the water. Sara, Tarig, and Mona ran from house to house, telling people to move to the school, which stood on higher ground.

Hardly had the last family reached the school when the water poured into the empty streets behind them. Two hundred people were crowded into four classrooms, most of them wet and frightened. Then a woman ran to Sara. "My father needs his heart medicine," she said, "and it's in our house." The house was already under water.

Sara called the one person she knew who could get medicine through a flood. Omar's company had spent a year testing drones that carry medicine to villages. "Give me two hours," he said. "Keep your phone on."

Only then did Sara realize how tired she was, but there was no time to rest. Mona kept the children calm with games and stories. Tarig connected the batteries from the pump to the school, so the classrooms had light all night. The women cooked rice in the yard, and the men carried clean water from the pump's tank. Everyone had a job. "Many hands make light work," said one of the old men.

At two in the morning, they heard a soft buzzing above the school. A small drone came down out of the darkness and landed in the yard with a box. Inside were the medicine, some bandages, and a note. From Omar's Technology. With an H this time. Sara laughed for the first time that night.

By the next afternoon, the water had gone down, and a Red Crescent truck arrived. Never before had the village felt so close. "You were a ray of hope for us," the woman told Sara. Sara shook her head and pointed at the people in the yard. "No," she said. "We all were."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where was Sara?In the village near Kassala, where her team had built the solar pump.
2
What had the old men never seen?So much rain in one afternoon.
3
What did the Gash River become?A brown, roaring wall of water.
4
What happened to the road to Kassala?It was cut off within an hour.
5
Where did the families go?To the school, which stood on higher ground.
6
What happened as soon as the last family reached the school?The water poured into the empty streets behind them.
7
What did the woman's father need?His heart medicine.
8
Who did Sara call?Omar.
9
How did the classrooms have light all night?Tarig connected the batteries from the pump to the school.
10
When did the drone arrive?At two in the morning.
11
What did the note say?From Omar's Technology. With an H this time.
12
What did Sara say when the woman thanked her?"We all were."

3Point of view Now Mona tells it.

MO

I have worked on many projects, but never have I been as frightened as I was that night. The rain didn't stop for six hours, and the river rose faster than any of us expected.

My job was the children. More than eighty of them were in one classroom, terrified of the noise, so we played games and sang until they fell asleep. Not once did they stop asking about their homes.

Little did we know that Omar was already on his way. When his drone landed in the yard, the children who were still awake started cheering, and the ones who were asleep woke up.

Only later did I understand what we had done. Nobody had been hurt, and every family had a dry place to sleep.

4What did you learn?

You learned inversion for emphasis.

After a negative or limiting word at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary verb comes before the subject, as in a question. It sounds formal and dramatic.

Normal word orderWith inversion
The village had never seen such rain.Never had the village seen such rain.
The river rose, and the road closed too.Not only did the river rise, but…
As soon as they arrived, the water came.Hardly had they arrived when it came.
She realized it only then.Only then did she realize it.
We didn't know he was coming.Little did we know he was coming.
Word + auxiliary + subjectNever have I seen… Rarely do we hear… Not once did they stop…
Past simple: add didThe river rose. Not only did the river rise…
Use it carefullyIt is dramatic. In everyday speech, normal word order is better.
QuestionsWhat have you never seen in your life?Never have I seen snow.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasecut off

separated from other places, so that people can't reach you

After the storm, the village was cut off for three days.
proverbMany hands make light work.

A job is easier and faster when many people help.

Let's all clean the classroom together. Many hands make light work.
idioma ray of hope

a small sign that things will get better

The doctor's words gave the family a ray of hope.

6New words

roaringmaking a very loud, deep noise
pouredflowed quickly and in large amounts
crowdedwith too many people in a small space
bandageslong pieces of cloth that you put around a wound
buzzinga low noise like the sound of a bee
terrifiedvery, very frightened

Science · Lesson 5

Why the Nile Floods

How rain on mountains far away fills a river in one of the driest places on Earth, and why the flood is both a gift and a danger.

Explain a natural processUse inversion in formal writingTalk about the good and bad sides of nature

1Read

Every summer, the Nile rises. For thousands of years, the people along its banks have waited for this flood, and feared it. But why does a river in one of the driest parts of the world flood at all?

The answer lies far to the south and east, in the Ethiopian Highlands. From June to September, monsoon winds carry heavy rain from the Indian Ocean to these mountains. The water rushes down into the Blue Nile, which starts at Lake Tana, and into other rivers like the Atbara. Only in these months does the Blue Nile become a giant.

The White Nile, which comes from the great lakes of East Africa, is very different. Its water travels slowly through huge swamps in South Sudan, where much of it is lost to the sun. Rarely does it rise quickly. The two rivers meet at Khartoum, and in the flood season, most of the water that reaches Egypt comes from Ethiopia.

For farmers, the flood has always been a double-edged sword. It leaves behind silt, a rich, dark soil that makes the fields green, and people in ancient times even built stone steps to measure the river and predict the harvest. But the flood can also destroy. In 2020, the Blue Nile at Khartoum reached its highest level in more than a hundred years, and thousands of homes were swept away.

Today, dams like the Roseires Dam in Sudan and the Aswan High Dam in Egypt control much of the flood. They store water and make electricity. But no dam can control the rain. As the climate changes, scientists warn that heavy floods may come more often, so cities along the river need better plans, stronger homes, and early warnings.

2Where the flood water comes from

June to Septembermonsoon rain on the Ethiopian Highlands
Blue Nilebrings most of the flood water
White Nileslower, loses water in the swamps
Khartoumwhere the two rivers meet
Did you know?

After they meet at Khartoum, the Blue Nile and the White Nile flow side by side for a while, and from the bridges you can see their two different colors.

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where does the flood water come from?The Ethiopian Highlands.
2
When does the heavy rain fall?From June to September.
3
Where does the Blue Nile start?At Lake Tana.
4
Why does the White Nile rarely rise quickly?Its water travels through huge swamps, where much of it is lost to the sun.
5
Where do the two rivers meet?At Khartoum.
6
What is silt?A rich, dark soil that the flood leaves behind.
7
What happened in 2020?The Blue Nile at Khartoum reached its highest level in more than a hundred years.
8
What do dams do?They store water, make electricity, and control much of the flood.

4Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idioma double-edged sword

something that has both good and bad results

Social media is a double-edged sword. It connects us, but it also wastes our time.
phrasebe swept away

to be carried away by fast water or wind

During the storm, several boats were swept away.

5New words

banksthe land along the sides of a river
monsoona wind that brings heavy rain in summer
swampsareas of soft, wet land
predictsay what will happen in the future
harvestthe time when farmers collect their crops
warningsmessages that tell people about a danger

Asking for More Time

Making a formal request and agreeing on a compromise

Make a formal requestExplain your reasonsAccept a compromise

1Read the conversation

After the flood, Sara is late with her final report. She goes to see her professor, Dr. Malik.
SSARAGood morning, Dr. Malik. Do you have a moment?
DMDR. MALIKOf course, Sara. Come in. How is the village after the flood?
SSARAEveryone is safe, thank you. But that's actually why I'm here. I was wondering whether it would be possible to have more time for my final report.
DMDR. MALIKI see. The deadline is this Thursday. How much time do you need?
SSARAWould two weeks be acceptable? I spent five days helping in the village, and I've fallen behind with my data.
DMDR. MALIKTwo weeks is a lot. Could you finish in ten days if I gave you the data from last year's project?
SSARAThat would really help. Not only would I save time, but I could also compare the two years.
DMDR. MALIKThen ten days it is. Send me a short plan by Sunday, so I know you're on track.
SSARAThank you so much. That's a weight off my shoulders.
DMDR. MALIKYou did something important in that village, Sara. Now go and write about it.

2Useful phrases

Ask for a moment

Do you have a moment?

Make a formal request

I was wondering whether it would be possible to have more time.

Explain the reason

I spent five days helping in the village.

Suggest an amount

Would two weeks be acceptable?

Accept a compromise

That would really help.

Thank someone warmly

Thank you so much.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasefall behind

to do less than you should by a certain time

I was sick for a week, and I fell behind with my homework.
idioma weight off your shoulders

the feeling of relief when a worry goes away

When I paid back the money, it was a weight off my shoulders.

4New words

reporta piece of writing about what you have studied or found
deadlinethe last day or time to finish something
acceptablegood enough to agree to
datafacts and numbers that you collect
comparelook at two things to see how they are different
on trackdoing what you planned to do

Story · Lesson 7

The App That Went Wrong

Omar's new app for farmers goes live and sends the wrong prices to everyone. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of his youngest engineer.

Use conditionals without ifTalk about mistakes and responsibilityTell a story about a crisis at work

1The story

For six months, Omar's team had been building FarmPrice, an app that tells farmers the latest prices in the big markets, so that nobody can cheat them. Should the price of onions rise in Omdurman, a farmer two hundred kilometers away will know within minutes.

The launch was planned for Monday. On Sunday night, Amir, the youngest engineer, asked for one more week of testing. Omar said no. The radio had already announced the launch, and three hundred farmers were waiting. Look before you leap, Amir thought, but he said nothing.

At nine o'clock on Monday, FarmPrice went live. By ten, the phones were ringing. A farmer in Gezira had sold his tomatoes for half their price, because the app said that the market price had fallen. Another had driven to Khartoum to sell onions at a price that didn't exist. By lunchtime, the news had spread like wildfire on social media.

Omar couldn't find the problem, and neither could his team. Then, at four o'clock, he got a message from Huda. "My students think they've found your mistake," it said. Huda had been using the app in her class to teach numbers and prices, and a nine-year-old girl had noticed that it was mixing up the price of one kilo with the price of a whole box.

The team fixed it in twenty minutes. Had they tested the app for one more week, they would have found the mistake themselves. Were it not for a class of nine-year-olds, it might have taken days.

That evening, Omar did the hardest thing he had ever done in business. He went on the radio and owned up to the mistake. "Had I listened to my youngest engineer," he said, "this would never have happened. Should any farmer have lost money today, my company will pay it back."

A month later, FarmPrice had five thousand users, more than Omar had ever hoped for. "People forgive mistakes," Mr. Ali told him. "What they don't forgive is hiding them." And at Huda's school, a nine-year-old girl now has a certificate on her wall. It says Chief Tester.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
What does FarmPrice do?It tells farmers the latest prices in the big markets.
2
When was the launch planned?For Monday.
3
What did Amir ask for?One more week of testing.
4
Why did Omar say no?The radio had already announced the launch, and three hundred farmers were waiting.
5
What happened to the farmer in Gezira?He sold his tomatoes for half their price.
6
How did the news travel?It spread like wildfire on social media.
7
Who sent Omar a message at four o'clock?Huda.
8
What had a nine-year-old girl noticed?The app was mixing up the price of one kilo with the price of a whole box.
9
How long did it take to fix the mistake?Twenty minutes.
10
What did Omar do on the radio?He owned up to the mistake.
11
What did he promise?That his company would pay back any farmer who had lost money.
12
What does the girl's certificate say?Chief Tester.

3Point of view Now Amir tells it.

AM

On Sunday night, I asked Omar for one more week. Had he said yes, we would have found the mistake ourselves. But the radio had already announced the launch, and were I in his place, I might have done the same.

On Monday, I watched our phones ring all day. Every call was a farmer who had lost money because of our app, and I felt sick.

When Huda's message arrived, I read it three times. A child had found in one afternoon what six engineers had missed for six months.

What I will remember most, though, is Omar on the radio. He didn't blame me, and he didn't blame the code. He said that it was his decision. Should I ever start my own company, I will try to be that kind of boss.

4What did you learn?

You learned conditionals without if.

In formal English, we can drop if and put had, should, or were first. The meaning doesn't change.

With ifWithout if
If they had tested it, …Had they tested it, …
If I had listened, …Had I listened, …
If any farmer has lost money, …Should any farmer have lost money, …
If I were in his place, …Were I in his place, …
If it weren't for the children, …Were it not for the children, …
Had = if + past perfectHad I known, I would have come.
Should = if, for a possible futureShould you need help, call me.
Were = if + wereWere I you, I would wait.
QuestionsWhat would you have done, had you been Omar?Had I been Omar, I would have waited one more week.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

proverbLook before you leap.

Think carefully about the results before you do something.

Don't sign the contract today. Read it first. Look before you leap.
idiomspread like wildfire

to travel very quickly from person to person

The news of the free concert spread like wildfire.
phraseown up to

to admit that you did something wrong

Nobody owned up to breaking the window.

6New words

cheatget something from someone in a way that is not honest
launchthe day a new product is first offered to people
announcedtold everyone in public
userspeople who use a product or a service
certificatean official paper that says you have done something
blamesay that someone is responsible for something bad

Podcast · Lesson 8

Can You Believe What You Read Online?

A newspaper reporter explains why fake news spreads so fast, and how to check a story before you share it.

Follow a podcast discussionTalk about fake newsUse should and had without if

1Before you listen

Have you ever shared something online and then found out that it wasn't true?

How do you decide whether a news story is real?

2Listen and read The Future Vision Podcast · Episode 24

Hosts: Sara and Adam · Guest: Rania Hamid, a reporter at The Daily Nile
00:05SSARAWelcome to The Future Vision Podcast. I'm Sara.
00:08AADAMAnd I'm Adam. Today we're talking about fake news. Our guest is Rania Hamid, a reporter at The Daily Nile. Welcome, Rania!
00:16RRANIAThank you. Actually, Sara and I have met before, at a conference in Cairo.
00:21SSARAThe one where I lost my laptop! So, Rania, why does fake news spread so fast?
00:27RRANIABecause it's designed to make us feel something, like fear, anger, or surprise. A shocking story can go viral in an hour, long before anyone checks it.
00:39AADAMLast month, my uncle sent me a message saying that bananas cure headaches. He'd shared it with forty people.
00:47RRANIAThat's a perfect example. Had he checked one good source, he would have found that it wasn't true.
00:55SSARASo what should we do?
00:57RRANIAThree things. First, look at the source. Who wrote it, and when? Second, should you see a shocking headline, read the whole article before you share it. And third, take it with a pinch of salt if no other news website is reporting it.
01:16AADAMWhat about photos and videos? They look so real.
01:20RRANIAThey can be old, or changed with software. Were I a student today, I'd learn how to search for a photo online and see where it first appeared.
01:33SSARAHave you ever been fooled yourself?
01:36RRANIAOnce, early in my career. I almost published a story about a lion in a Khartoum market. Luckily, my editor asked me to find one person who had actually seen it. Nobody had.
01:50AADAMA lion in the market! I would have shared that.
01:53RRANIAThat's exactly the problem. The best stories are often the ones we should check twice.
02:00SSARARania, thank you so much. That's all for today. Next week, we're talking about the future of farming. See you then!

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Who is the guest?Rania Hamid, a reporter at The Daily Nile.
2
Where had Sara and Rania met before?At a conference in Cairo.
3
Why does fake news spread so fast?It's designed to make us feel something, like fear, anger, or surprise.
4
What did Adam's uncle share?A message saying that bananas cure headaches.
5
What should you do if you see a shocking headline?Read the whole article before you share it.
6
What would Rania learn if she were a student today?How to search for a photo online and see where it first appeared.
7
What story did Rania almost publish?A story about a lion in a Khartoum market.
8
Which stories should we check twice?The best stories.

phrasego viral

to be shared very quickly by a lot of people online

idiomtake something with a pinch of salt

to not completely believe something

ADVANCED 3Unit 4 · Lesson 9
Story · Lesson 9

Two Offers

Adam gets two job offers on the same day, one far away and one at home. Read the story, then read it from his grandfather's point of view.

Talk about wishes and regretsSay what you would rather someone didTalk about a difficult choice

1The story

On the same Tuesday, Adam received two emails. The first was from a large airline in the Gulf. They were offering him a place as a junior pilot, with a salary five times bigger than anything in Sudan, and the chance to fly some of the biggest planes in the world. The second was from Sudan's national airline. The salary was small, and the planes were old, but the job was in Khartoum.

"It's the chance of a lifetime," said Omar. "If you don't go, I'll go for you." Sara wasn't so sure. "I'd rather you stayed," she said honestly. "But I'd rather you were happy there than unhappy here."

For a week, Adam couldn't sleep. Every night, he sat at his desk and tried to weigh up the two offers on a piece of paper. Money, planes, and experience on one side. Family, friends, and the Nile on the other. "I wish I could be in two places at once," he told Huda. "If only someone would make the decision for me."

Finally, he went to see Mr. Ali. He knew the story of the bank job in Dubai, and he expected his old teacher to tell him to stay. Instead, Mr. Ali surprised him. "My choice was right for me," he said. "It doesn't have to be right for you. It's time you stopped asking other people and asked yourself."

Then Adam went to his grandparents' house. His grandfather listened quietly. "When I left for Cairo in 1975," he said, "I wished every day that I hadn't gone. But I came back a better engineer, and your grandmother waited. Home is where the heart is, Adam. If your heart is here, it will bring you back."

That night, Adam made his decision. He would fly in the Gulf for five years, learn everything he could, and then come home to fly for Sudan. He called the national airline and asked if they would hold a place for him. "We'd rather you started now," the manager said. "But we'll be waiting."

At the airport, his grandmother gave him a small envelope. Inside was the letter from 1975. "Keep it," she said. "It reminds us that some people are worth coming back for."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How many emails did Adam receive?Two.
2
What was the first offer?A place as a junior pilot at a large airline in the Gulf.
3
What was good about the second offer?The job was in Khartoum.
4
What did Omar say?It's the chance of a lifetime.
5
What did Sara say?She'd rather he stayed, but she'd rather he was happy there than unhappy here.
6
What did Adam write on one side of the paper?Money, planes, and experience.
7
What did Adam wish?That he could be in two places at once.
8
What did he expect Mr. Ali to tell him?To stay.
9
What did Mr. Ali tell him?It was time he stopped asking other people and asked himself.
10
What did his grandfather say about home?Home is where the heart is.
11
What did Adam decide?To fly in the Gulf for five years and then come home to fly for Sudan.
12
What did his grandmother give him at the airport?The letter from 1975.

3Point of view Now Adam's grandfather tells it.

G

When Adam came to see me, he looked exactly like I did in 1975, young, excited, and afraid. He wished someone would tell him what to do.

I didn't tell him. I'd rather he made his own mistakes than lived with mine. But I told him the truth. Leaving was the hardest thing I ever did, and it was also the best.

I wish I had written more letters home when I was in Cairo. I hope Adam writes more than I did.

When Amna gave him the letter at the airport, I had to look away. It's high time I stopped crying at airports. I am seventy-one years old.

4What did you learn?

You learned wish, if only, would rather, and it's time.

We use them to talk about what we want to be different. After them, we often use a past form, even when we mean now.

FormExample
I wish + past: about nowI wish I could be in two places.
I wish + past perfect: a regretI wish I had written more letters.
If only … wouldIf only someone would decide for me!
I'd rather + person + pastI'd rather you stayed.
It's time + person + pastIt's time you stopped asking others.
A past form with a present meaningI'd rather you stayed means: I want you to stay now.
I'd rather + verb, for yourselfI'd rather fly for Sudan. I'd rather you flew for Sudan.
It's high time is strongerIt's high time we left. We are very late.
QuestionsWhat do you wish you could change about your city?I wish there were more parks.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomthe chance of a lifetime

a very good opportunity that you will probably never get again

Studying at that famous school was the chance of a lifetime.
phraseweigh up

to think carefully about the good and bad sides before you decide

Before buying the car, she weighed up the price and the cost of the fuel.
proverbHome is where the heart is.

Your real home is the place where the people you love are.

She has lived in three countries, but she always says that home is where the heart is.

juniorat a low level in a job because you are new
nationalbelonging to the whole country
experienceknowledge and skill that you get from doing something
holdkeep something for someone until later
remindsmakes someone remember something
worthgood or important enough for something

News · Lesson 10

More Graduates Look for Work Abroad

Read a news report about young people leaving to work in other countries, and the ones who plan to come back.

Read an education reportFind who, what, where, when, and whyNotice it's time and would rather in formal English

1Read the article

The Daily NileSunday, June 14

More Young Graduates Look for Work Abroad

A new survey shows that four in ten graduates plan to leave the country, but many say that they would rather come home later.

By our education reporter

Four in ten young graduates are planning to work abroad, according to a new survey of two thousand students in their final year. Most of them hope to find jobs in the Gulf, in Europe, or in other African countries.

The main reason, the survey found, is money. Many graduates say that salaries at home are too low to make ends meet, especially in medicine, engineering, and technology. "I love my country," said one medical student, "but I have to think about my family."

Experts have long warned about the brain drain, the loss of skilled people to other countries. "Every doctor who leaves is a hospital that waits longer," said a professor of medicine. "It is time the government made it easier for young people to stay."

“Every doctor who leaves is a hospital that waits longer.”A professor of medicine

But the survey also found some good news. More than half of the graduates who plan to leave say that they would rather come back within ten years, bringing new skills and experience with them. Some companies are already trying to attract them home. One airline, for example, has started to hold places for young pilots who train abroad.

"Leaving is not always a loss," said a young engineer who returned last year after five years in Germany. "I learned things there that I could never have learned here. Now I'm teaching them to others."

2The five key facts

Who?young graduates in their final year
What?four in ten plan to work abroad
Where?the Gulf, Europe, and other African countries
When?a new survey this year
Why?low salaries at home

3

4
What is the brain drain?The loss of skilled people to other countries.
5
What does the professor say it is time for?For the government to make it easier for young people to stay.
6
What would more than half of them rather do?Come back within ten years.
7
What has one airline started to do?Hold places for young pilots who train abroad.

to have just enough money for the things you need

when many educated or skilled people leave their country to work in another

The country lost many of its doctors to the brain drain.

5New words

Conversation · Lesson 11

Negotiating a Job Offer

Asking politely for better terms before you sign

Discuss the terms of a job offerMake polite requestsAgree on a compromise

1Read the conversation

Before he signs his contract, Adam talks to Ms. Layla, the head of training at the airline in the Gulf.
MLMS. LAYLAAdam, we're very happy that you want to accept our offer. Do you have any questions before you sign?
AADAMThank you. I'm excited to join you. There are just two things I'd like to discuss, if that's all right.
MLMS. LAYLAOf course. Go ahead.
AADAMThe first is the start date. The offer says September 1, but my final exams finish on September 10. Would you be open to a start date of October 1?
MLMS. LAYLAOur training course begins in September, so that's difficult. Could you start on September 15? You would join the course one week late.
AADAMThat works for me. Thank you for meeting me halfway.
MLMS. LAYLAAnd the second thing?
AADAMThe contract is for three years, but I'd rather sign for five. After that, I'd like to know whether I could leave without paying back the cost of my training.
MLMS. LAYLAThat's an unusual question, but a fair one. If you stay five years, we pay for all of your training. I'll put that in writing, and then the ball is in your court.
AADAMThen I'm ready to sign. Thank you, Ms. Layla.

2Useful phrases

Say you have questions

There are just two things I'd like to discuss, if that's all right.

Make a request

Would you be open to a start date of October 1?

Accept a compromise

That works for me.

Say what you prefer

I'd rather sign for five years.

Ask about a condition

I'd like to know whether I could leave without paying back the cost.

Close the deal

Then I'm ready to sign.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasemeet someone halfway

to agree to part of what someone wants, so that you both get something

I wanted 100 pounds and he offered 60, so we met halfway at 80.
idiomthe ball is in your court

it is your turn to decide or act

I've sent you my best price. Now the ball is in your court.

4New words

acceptsay yes to something that is offered
signwrite your name on a paper to show you agree
discusstalk about something with someone
contracta written agreement between people or companies
unusualdifferent from what is normal
fairright and reasonable

ADVANCED 3Unit 5 · Lesson 12
Story · Lesson 12

The Last Lesson

After thirty years, Mr. Ali is teaching his last class. He hates being thanked, so his students find another way. Read the story, then read it from Mr. Ali's point of view.

Use advanced passive formsTalk about memories and endingsSay thank you in a meaningful way

1The story

After thirty years, Mr. Ali's last day at the institute had come. He had asked for no party and no speeches, because Mr. Ali hates being thanked. "Teachers are paid to teach," he always said. "They don't need to be thanked for it."

So his students decided not to thank him, not with words, anyway. For two months, Huda and Sara had been secretly contacting people who had been taught by him over the years. They found more than two hundred.

On the last day, Mr. Ali walked into his classroom at eight o'clock, as usual, and stopped. The room was full. Doctors, farmers, engineers, shop owners, and teachers were sitting at the desks, and more were standing along the walls. On the board, someone had written one word. Future.

"Having been taught by you," said Dr. Amira, standing up, "we wanted to give you one more lesson. Today, you're the student." And one by one, they told him what they had learned from him. Not grammar, but other things. To ask questions. To be patient. To stop for people by the road. Omar said that one, and everyone laughed.

Mr. Ali tried to speak, but he had a lump in his throat. Then Adam, who had been given three days off by his new airline, stood up with a box. Inside were the letters that the class had written to their future selves. "You were supposed to post these in ten years," he said. "But we'd like you to read them now."

Mr. Ali read them all, slowly, while the room waited. Then he put them back in the box. "Every one of you has become what you wrote," he said quietly. "I expected to be given a cake today, not this."

When he finally left the building, his students walked with him to the gate. "Will you miss it?" asked Sara. Mr. Ali smiled. "When I look back on these thirty years, I will remember faces, not lessons. All good things must come to an end. But that doesn't mean they stop being good."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How long had Mr. Ali been teaching at the institute?Thirty years.
2
What had he asked for?No party and no speeches.
3
Why doesn't he like being thanked?He says that teachers are paid to teach.
4
What had Huda and Sara been doing for two months?Secretly contacting people who had been taught by him.
5
How many did they find?More than two hundred.
6
What did Mr. Ali see when he walked into his classroom?The room was full of his old students.
7
What word was written on the board?Future.
8
What did Dr. Amira say?Today, you're the student.
9
What did Omar say he had learned?To stop for people by the road.
10
What was inside Adam's box?The letters that the class had written to their future selves.
11
What did Mr. Ali expect to be given?A cake.
12
What will he remember when he looks back on these years?Faces, not lessons.

3Point of view Now Mr. Ali tells it.

MA

I don't like being surprised, and I hate being thanked. My students know both of these things, so of course they did both.

When I opened the door that morning, I saw thirty years of faces. Some of them I had taught as children, and now they were being called doctor and engineer by their own students.

Having been told for thirty years that teaching is a small job, I learned that day that it is not. Every person in that room had been changed by something small, a question, a word on a board, a little patience.

I am told that I will be given a pension and a quiet life. I would rather be given a new class. But perhaps it is time I learned something new myself.

4What did you learn?

You learned advanced passive forms.

The passive can come after verbs and in other forms, not only after is and was.

FormExample
being + past participleHe hates being thanked.
to be + past participleThey don't need to be thanked.
having been + past participleHaving been taught by you, we…
had been + past participlePeople who had been taught by him came.
was / were being + past participleThey were being called doctor.
After like, hate, enjoy: beingI don't like being surprised.
After want, expect, need: to beI expected to be given a cake.
Who did it? Add byThey had been taught by Mr. Ali.
QuestionsDo you like being given advice?I like being given advice by my parents.

5Idioms, proverbs and phrases

idiomhave a lump in your throat

to feel that you are going to cry

When my sister got married, I had a lump in my throat.
phraselook back on something

to think about something that happened in the past

When I look back on my school days, I remember my friends most.
proverbAll good things must come to an end.

Even the best times in life don't last forever.

The holiday was wonderful, but all good things must come to an end.

6New words

speechesformal talks to a group of people
secretlywithout other people knowing
contactingcalling or writing to someone
ownerspeople who have something that belongs to them
patiencethe ability to wait or try again without getting angry
pensionmoney that you get every month after you stop working

The Scholarship Interview

Answering a panel's questions about your plans for study

Explain your reasons for further studyDescribe a research planAnswer a difficult question calmly

1Read the conversation

Huda has an interview for a scholarship to study a master's degree in education. Dr. Nabil and Dr. Amira are on the panel.
DNDR. NABILGood afternoon, Huda. Why do you want to study for a master's degree in education?
HHUDAHaving taught for two years, I've realized how much I still don't know. I'd like to be given the chance to learn how children really learn.
DADR. AMIRAWhat has been the most difficult part of your teaching?
HHUDAChildren who are afraid to speak. What I've learned is that they need to be noticed, not pushed.
DNDR. NABILAnd what would you research, were you given the scholarship?
HHUDAHow stories help shy children speak a new language. I've seen it in my class, but I'd like to prove it properly.
DADR. AMIRASome people say that research changes nothing in real classrooms. What do you think?
HHUDAI try to keep an open mind. But had I not tried new ideas, a boy in my class would still be hiding under his desk.
DNDR. NABILThank you, Huda. We'll let you know within two weeks.
HHUDAThank you for your time. Studying here would be a dream come true.

2Useful phrases

Explain your reason

Having taught for two years, I've realized how much I still don't know.

Say what you would like

I'd like to be given the chance to learn.

Share what you have learned

What I've learned is that they need to be noticed.

3Idioms, proverbs and phrases

phrasekeep an open mind

to be ready to listen to new ideas before you decide

idioma dream come true

something that you have wanted for a very long time

Visiting Japan was a dream come true for my brother.

4New words

scholarshipmoney that is given to a student to pay for study
master's degreea university degree that you study for after your first degree
panela small group of people who ask questions and make a decision
researchcareful study to find out new facts
